key_insight: Large language models can nearly match expert-level reliability and outperform lay annotators when judging empathic communication—provided the evaluation criteria are clear and specific.
problem_solved: Scalable, consistent assessment of empathic communication is limited by costly expert raters and high variability among lay annotators; this paper shows LLMs can be a reliable, lower-cost alternative when guided by precise rubrics.
method: Compare judgment performance and inter-rater reliability of LLMs, expert annotators, and laypeople across multiple empathic communication frameworks.
Evaluate outcomes under different levels of rubric clarity to measure how specific evaluation criteria affect reliability.
Analyze agreement and error patterns to identify where LLMs match experts and where human oversight remains necessary.
impact: Enables more scalable and consistent evaluation of empathy in conversational systems and communication research, reducing dependence on costly experts—while emphasizing that rubric design is crucial for trustworthy automated judgments.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing reliability scores (LLMs vs experts vs laypeople) across frameworks
Flow diagram of the evaluation pipeline: prompt/rubric → rater type → judgments → reliability analysis
Illustration showing rubric clarity gradient (vague → specific) and corresponding change in LLM/expert agreement
Radar chart showing performance across multiple empathic dimensions or frameworks
paper_title: When large language models are reliable for judging empathic communication
paper_authors: Aakriti Kumar, Nalin Poungpeth, Diyi Yang, Erina Farrell, Bruce L. Lambert
